passage:
Lavanya, sit down, I'll tell you why I never forward anything the moment it arrives. I'm Aparna, and I was a young woman of twenty-four, waiting at the bus stop across from Bhaskar's stationery shop. A voice note was going round the phones: a child had been taken from that shop. Within minutes forty people stood outside, shouting, some pushing at the shutter. Bhaskar stood behind his counter, pale, hands raised, unable to speak.

I couldn't say what was true. I only knew that nobody near me had seen anything. I rang the police and said only what I could see: a crowd and a frightened shopkeeper. The van arrived, and an hour later the child's mother walked up with the child in her arms. She had been at the pharmacy next door. By then Bhaskar's glass door was cracked.

qa.q: Where was Aparna waiting when the voice note went round?
qa.a: Aparna was waiting at the bus stop across from Bhaskar's stationery shop.

qa.q: What was Bhaskar feeling, standing behind the counter with hands raised?
qa.a: Bhaskar was frightened and helpless, pale and unable to speak while a crowd he had never harmed shouted at him.

qa.q: What did Aparna do when unable to tell what was true?
qa.a: Aparna rang the police and said only what could be seen: a crowd and a frightened shopkeeper.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for Bhaskar afterwards, with the cracked glass door?
qa.a: Bhaskar probably felt shaken and hurt, since the crowd had believed a false story so fast, and the cracked door would be a reminder.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a rumour on phones turn a crowd against an innocent shopkeeper while verified facts arrived too late.

passage:
Rain hammered the station roof and the night train was two hours late. On the crowded platform Eshaan's phone buzzed with a forwarded message: “A woman is carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.” Below it was a photo of Ira, taken from behind, a sleeping girl on her shoulder.

Within minutes a ring of men had gathered. “Where are you taking her?” “Show us the ticket!” Ira clutched the child, eyes wide, trying to speak over the voices. Nobody had waited for facts.

Eshaan looked at the message again: no name, no sender, nothing checkable. Eshaan walked to the railway guard. “There's a crowd around a woman with a child. Please come.” The guard arrived and asked calmly whether someone could be called for the child. Ten minutes later a woman ran in, dripping wet. “That's my sister! She's been holding my daughter while I bought tickets.”

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: The message claimed a woman was carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling, clutching the child with wide eyes?
qa.a: Ira was frightened and helpless, trying to speak while a ring of men shouted, and nobody waited for facts.

qa.q: What choice did Eshaan make instead of joining the crowd?
qa.a: Eshaan noticed the message had no name or sender and asked the railway guard to come, rather than confronting Ira.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ira when the woman ran in and said the child was her daughter?
qa.a: Ira likely felt huge relief but also shaken and humiliated, since strangers had accused Ira before checking anything.

grounding: An observer watches a rumour on a messaging app turn a station crowd against an innocent woman, and facts arrive after the outrage has begun.

From her third-floor balcony in the Delhi colony, Deepika saw the crowd forming around a thin man with a clipboard near the park gate.
Her neighbour Bhavna called up, holding her phone. “There's a message! A child-lifter with a clipboard, pretending to do surveys!” The message had a blurry photo that could have been anyone.
Below, twenty people had become forty. Someone grabbed the man's collar. He was shouting, “I'm from the municipal survey!” Nobody listened.
Deepika's hands went cold. She dialled 112 and gave the address, then ran down with her own ID card from work, which looked just like his.
The police van arrived in six minutes and pulled the man into the vehicle, safe. An hour later, the municipal office posted that the survey was real. By then the message had been shared a thousand times.

qa.q: How many minutes did the police van take to arrive?
qa.a: It arrived in six minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling as she watched the crowd grow?
qa.a: Her hands went cold; she felt frightened and alarmed as the rumour turned a crowd against an innocent man.

qa.q: What steps did Deepika take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: She called 112 with the address straight away and went down with an ID card like his, getting protection there without joining the crowd.

qa.q: How might the survey worker have felt when nobody listened?
qa.a: He was likely terrified and helpless, shouting the truth while a crowd grabbed him because of a blurry photo.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a messaging rumour turn a crowd angry at an innocent survey worker, with verified facts arriving late.

passage:
“Avni, look, they're beating the delivery man!” Charu grabbed her arm at the vegetable market.
“What happened?”
“Someone posted in the market group that he hit a child with his bike and drove off.”
A dozen men had surrounded the rider. One slapped him. He was holding up his hands. “I didn't! I stopped to help!”
Avni's heart hammered. “Charu, call the police. I'll find the child.”
She pushed through to a woman holding a crying boy with a scraped knee. “Did the bike hit him?”
“No,” the mother said, startled. “He fell running. That man picked him up.”
Avni shouted it, twice, as loud as she could. The men hesitated. The police jeep arrived five minutes later. By then the rider's lip was bleeding.

qa.q: What did the post in the market group claim?
qa.a: It claimed he hit a child with his bike and drove off.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when her heart hammered?
qa.a: She felt alarmed and scared, seeing a crowd attack a man on the basis of a rumour.

qa.q: What did Avni and Charu do that helped?
qa.a: Charu called the police while Avni found the mother and shouted the real facts, which made the men hesitate.

qa.q: How might the child's mother have felt hearing what the crowd did?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and upset, since the man they were beating had actually helped her son.

grounding: Shows observers watching a group-chat rumour turn a market crowd against an innocent delivery rider before the facts arrive.

passage:
I'm Imran, and I still dream about that evening in our town.
A message came into every group: a stranger had poisoned the water tank near the mosque. It had a voice note, a man crying. People believed it immediately.
By eight, a crowd had cornered a young man with a backpack near the bus stand. He was from out of town, looking for his uncle's house. I watched from the tea stall with Indu, my colleague. Someone threw a stone.
I rang the police and the ward councillor. Indu called the water board.
The police came, took the young man away safely, and the water board tested the tank that night. Clean. The notice came out the next morning. By then, everyone had already decided who he was.

qa.q: Where was the young man cornered?
qa.a: Near the bus stand.

qa.q: How does Imran feel remembering that evening?
qa.a: Imran still feels shaken and haunted, dreaming about how fast the rumour turned people angry.

qa.q: What did Imran and Indu do that helped?
qa.a: They called the police, the ward councillor and the water board, so the young man was protected and the tank was tested.

qa.q: How might the young man with the backpack have felt?
qa.a: He was probably terrified and confused, just looking for his uncle's house when a crowd cornered him.

grounding: An observer recalls a messaging rumour turning a crowd against an innocent stranger, with verified facts arriving only after the outrage.

Incident note, primary health centre, Harigaon. Written by Zainab, community volunteer, 4 p.m.
At about 1 p.m. a forwarded voice message reached the village groups: "Child-lifters in a white van near the school. Stop them." By 1:30 around thirty people had surrounded Eshaan, a young surveyor measuring the road for the new drain, because his jeep was white. Someone grabbed his tape. The shouting grew as more people joined. Eshaan kept holding up his ID card; nobody looked at it.
I recognised his project letter from the panchayat notice board. I stood beside him, held the letter up high and asked the sarpanch's son to call the sarpanch and the police outpost. The police came at 2:10 and confirmed the survey. The message was two years old, from another district.
What I did next: I sat with Eshaan in the centre until he stopped shaking, and asked the sarpanch to send a correction to every village group this evening.

qa.q: Why did the crowd surround Eshaan?
qa.a: Because his jeep was white, matching the forwarded message.

qa.q: What was Zainab likely feeling while holding up the letter beside Eshaan?
qa.a: Zainab was probably frightened but determined, holding the facts while the crowd's anger was already rolling.

qa.q: Why was asking the sarpanch to send a correction important?
qa.a: The rumour was still sitting in every group; a clear correction from a trusted local voice could stop the next crowd.

qa.q: What was it like for Eshaan as the crowd grew?
qa.a: Eshaan was likely terrified and helpless, holding up an ID that nobody would even look at.

grounding: Shows an observer watching an old forwarded rumour turn a crowd against an innocent surveyor, with verified facts arriving only after the anger has started.
